title: Proactive KV-prefetch and kernel placement simulator
content:
Goal: prototype a lightweight simulator that lets us explore proactive KV prefetch strategies combined with kernel placement heuristics for heterogeneous stacks (Triton, TRT, custom ops). The focus is on tail latency behavior under streaming small requests, memory fragmentation from mixed kernels, and the cost/latency tradeoffs of prefetching prefixes into GPU memory vs on-demand KV retrieval.

Why this doc: we have lots of ad-hoc experiments (see linked PRs), but nobody has a compact sim that ties request arrival patterns, KV lifetime, and kernel residency together. This doc captures the proto model, a few runs, and recommended follow-ups. Intended for eng-serving-runtime folks and SREs who tune SLOs.

High-level hypothesis:
- Small streaming chat workloads benefit from selective proactive KV prefetch for hot prefixes; careful placement of compiled kernels (TRT) into dedicated memory slabs reduces tail spikes compared to naive on-demand loading.
- Over-aggressive prefetch increases GPU memory pressure and causes eviction churn that regresses p99.
- Triton-managed models are easier to multi-tenant but show higher cold-start overhead for custom TRT blobs unless we keep warm slabs.

Simulator design (quick notes):
- Event-driven single-process sim (Python prototype, ~300 LOC).
- Entities: request stream, model variants (triton container, TRT blob, custom-op), KV segments (prefix tokens mapped to KV shards), GPU nodes with memory pools and slab allocator, scheduler module implementing placement heuristics.
- Inputs: arrival trace (poisson + bursts), workload mix (chat short/long), per-model kernel size, cold-load time (TRT compile or blob load), KV size per prefix, KV fetch latency (host->GPU DMA or local cache), eviction policy.
- Outputs: p50/p95/p99 latency, average cost estimate (tokens*cost-per-op), memory occupancy trace, evictions per minute, cold starts/minute.

Key heuristics implemented:
1) Proactive-K (prefetch hot KV segments based on last-n requests frequency window).
2) Slab-reserve-TRT (reserve fixed slabs for TensorRT blobs and keep them resident up to a TTL).
3) On-demand-TRT (load TRT blob on first hit, with async background prewarm option).
4) Hybrid-evict (LRU for KV, size-aware for kernels; prefer evicting non-reserved TRT if eviction needed).
5) Kernel-placement-by-latency (assign latency-sensitive routes to nodes with reserved TRT slabs).

Experiment matrix (selected):
- Workloads: 70% short chat (<=80 tokens), 30% long chat (>=512 tokens) with burst windows of 200 RPS for 10s every 60s.
- Stack configs: Triton-only (dynamic), TRT-only (precompiled blobs), Mixed (TRT for 512+ sequences, Triton for short), Mixed+custom-op for specialized attention kernels.
- Prefetch policies: none, conservative (top-5 prefixes), aggressive (top-50 prefixes).
- Slab sizes: small (10% GPU mem), medium (25%), large (40%).

Representative results (proto numbers, sim runs seeded):
- Baseline (no prefetch, mixed stack): p99 = 530ms, cold-loads = 12/min, evictions = 18/min, avg mem usage = 72%
- Conservative prefetch + slab-reserve medium: p99 = 310ms, cold-loads = 3/min, evictions = 9/min, avg mem = 81% (+9% mem)
- Aggressive prefetch + no-reserve: p99 = 690ms (regression), cold-loads = 0/min, evictions = 45/min, avg mem = 93% (thrashing)
- TRT-only with slab large and conservative prefetch: p99 = 270ms, cost est = +12% vs baseline (higher infra cost due to larger reserved GPU footprint but lower tail)
- Triton-only: p99 = 420ms, cold-loads = 0/min (container resident) but higher mean latency for long sequences due to dynamic scheduling overhead

Initial takeaways (practical):
- Small, frequency-based prefetch window (top-5 to top-10 prefixes) gives robust tail reductions with minimal memory tax. Good starting default.
- If using TRT blobs, reserve modest slabs (20-30%) on a subset of GPU nodes and route latency-sensitive routes there. Keeps p99 low without reserving across the whole fleet.
- Avoid naive aggressive prefetch; add adaptive backoff based on observed eviction rate and p99.
- Triton provides operational simplicity for multitenant but expect higher median for long sequences; TRT wins on p99 when blobs are warm.

Operational considerations and tradeoffs:
- Cost vs latency: reserving slabs increases per-node cost (wasted capacity when underutilized). Need placement policy to only reserve on nodes with predictable commit/reserved capacity (Dedicated customers).
- Complexity vs benefit: Hybrid stack yields best SLOs but increases operational surface (blob management, versioning, fallback logic). Document lifecycle hooks: upload TRT artifact -> sign -> push to slab nodes -> health-check -> route.
- Eviction safety: build a safe-eviction mode where kernels have graceful unload: flush KV, send immediate fallback to Triton variant, instrument traces for rollback.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Can we cheaply derive hot-prefix sets from lightweight on-node counters instead of central telemetry? (reduce telemetry bandwidth)
- Probe TTL heuristics: TTL = f(request rate, kernel size) vs static TTL. Sim suggests dynamic TTL reduces evictions by ~20%. Need real trace runs.
- Evaluate benefit of small NVRAM hot-cache for KV on node vs GPU-resident prefetch. Simulated NVRAM cut p99 ~10% with moderate mem cost.
- Test split-kernel strategy: load small attention kernels as custom-op resident and load large matmul TRT blobs on demand. Initial sim promising but needs real bench.

Short TODOs (owner tags):
- Run sim with real traffic traces from prod (INF-1023) — Marcus Liu
- Wire up sim to sample-based profiler outputs (kernel size distribution) — Diego Ramos
- Add adaptive prefetch policy (eviction-aware) and rerun cost analysis — Anya Patel
- Draft rollout playbook for slab reservations and fallback routes — Priya Menon

Notes to self / rough log:
- Sim is intentionally approximate (no CUDA-level timing). Good for qualitative decisions and sizing only.
- Observed corner case: when two large TRT blobs compete and both get partially evicted, cold-reload storms amplified p99. Mitigation: staggered TTL jitter and inter-blob dependency awareness.
- Slack thread with early graphs: see linked_artifacts. Will upload sim code to runtime repo under tools/simulators once cleaned.

Recommended near-term default: conservative proactive prefetch (top-10), medium slab reserve on 10-20% of nodes dedicated to latency-sensitive routes, adaptive eviction backoff. Keep Triton fallback for all routes, add monitoring for eviction-induced p99 regressions.

If this resonates, I can turn the sim into an internal benchmarking harness that produces CSVs for the Console Optimize pipeline and a small RFC for rollout.

-- Anya
